basic_info.title: Advancing Map-Matching and Route Prediction: Challenges, Methods, and Unified Solutions
basic_info.authors: Tomasz Waksmundzki, Ewa Niewiadomska-Szynkiewicz, Janusz Granat (Institute of Control and Computation Engineering, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland)
basic_info.venue: MDPI Electronics, vol. 14, issue 18, article 3608, 2025 (published 11 September 2025; DOI 10.3390/electronics14183608). Special Issue: Big Data Analytics and Information Technology for Smart Cities and Citizen Wellbeing.

method.survey_scope_note: Review of AI-based map-matching and vehicle route-prediction methods. The survey proposes its own classification of map-matching algorithms by computational paradigm into three groups: (1) Spatio-Temporal Constraint approaches (deterministic geometric/topological rule-based: point-to-point, point-to-curve, curve-to-curve, topological constraints); (2) Inference Model-Based approaches (probabilistic estimation under noise: Particle Filters, Hidden Markov Models with emission/transition probabilities and Viterbi decoding, fuzzy logic, Dempster-Shafer theory); (3) Data-Driven / Learning approaches (machine learning and deep learning that learn spatial-temporal relationships). It surveys earlier taxonomies too (online vs offline / incremental vs global; geometric/topological/probabilistic/advanced; and the similarity / state-transition / candidate-evolving / scoring-model classification). Section 4 covers route-prediction algorithms and Section 5 covers multimodal sensor data fusion. The survey is descriptive, not a single proposed model; it argues conceptually for a unified map-matching + route-prediction framework (Figure 7, 'a conceptual diagram of the proposed integrated framework').

gap_analysis.whats_missing: The survey frames map-matching and route prediction as deeply coupled but historically tackled separately, and argues the field still lacks a single holistic framework that performs map-matching and route prediction jointly rather than as a disconnected pipeline (its central open direction). It stresses that classical methods (geometric/topological constraint and probabilistic HMM/particle-filter approaches) remain sensitive to GPS noise, the multipath effect, ambiguous/dense urban road layouts, and intersections, and that low-sampling-rate and low-quality trajectory data degrade accuracy. It positions deep learning as the more promising route for learning spatial-temporal dependencies and adapting to evolving traffic and diverse driver behaviour, while noting that effectively fusing multimodal sensor data into a unified situational-awareness model is an open challenge. NOTE: the precise wording of the Section 6 'future research directions' (and whether it explicitly names transformers, reinforcement learning, or label-free/self-supervised training as recommended directions) could not be verified from the fetched page because the equation-heavy Section 3 exhausted the page-fetch limit before Sections 4-6 were reached; these specific future-direction claims are therefore marked uncertain.
gap_analysis.novelty_reasoning: From verified content (abstract + Section 3 taxonomy + section structure) the survey describes a UNIFIED map-matching + route-prediction framework and deep learning as open/desirable directions, not as already-solved; it does not anywhere describe an existing transformer-encoder + latent-space-RL + label-free hybrid, so the thesis hybrid reads as a genuine open gap that this survey's unified-framework framing motivates rather than pre-empts. (Caveat: the exact future-research wording was not fully verifiable - see uncertain.)

relevance.bmw_relevance: A unified map-matching + route-prediction view lets BMW clean raw fleet GPS into accurate road-aligned trajectories and forecast likely future road segments within one model, improving downstream fleet analytics such as route optimisation, real-time traffic management, and demand/behaviour modelling.
